author: Riddhi Patel Santoki
title: The Neem Tree That Stayed — Two Basements Built Around It, in Sargasan
excerpt: At Sargasan, Gandhinagar, The Palm Group chose to save a mature neem tree standing beside two planned basements — instead of clearing it for a simpler build. Here's what that decision became.
body:
Every site has something on it before the drawings begin. At The Palm, in Sargasan, Gandhinagar, it was a neem tree — medium to large, fully grown, standing close to the driveway, slightly in front of where the society's entrance was planned. The project called for two basements, one of them double-height, with the tree sitting right beside that line. The decision came early: keep the tree, or clear it for a simpler, more convenient layout.

The Palm Group chose to keep it.

A neem tree that has grown into a site for years is not the same as a sapling that can be replanted elsewhere. It is native to this land, adapted to the soil and climate in a way no new planting can quickly replicate. Removing it would have meant losing shade, an established root network, and years of growth that no landscaping budget can buy back.

![Two-basement excavation at The Palm, Sargasan Gandhinagar, with neem tree preserved at site boundary](/images/uploads/neem-tree-basement-excavation-sargasan-gandhinagar.webp "Basement excavation with neem tree preserved – The Palm, Sargasan")

### What it means to design around what's already there

This is often the real tension in landscape design — a new planting scheme is easy to plan on an empty site, but a mature tree already standing on the plot forces a harder question: is it worth keeping, even when it's inconveniently placed? At The Palm, the neem tree stood close to the driveway, slightly in front of where the society's entrance was planned — not a minor detail to work around. Gujarat's older residential and institutional plots frequently carry neem, banyan, or peepal trees that predate any construction plan, and the easier decision is almost always to clear them for a cleaner, more convenient layout. Here, The Palm Group chose otherwise. In practice, the tree's position at the entrance has hardly registered as an obstruction for residents — it simply became part of arriving home.

### What the tree gives back today

The neem tree at The Palm now stands as one of the project's most-used outdoor spaces. Its canopy creates a naturally shaded area where residents sit and gather — dappled light, cooler air, a sense of permanence no umbrella or pergola replicates. Around it, a new landscape layer was planted to work with the tree rather than compete with it, and over time, this has grown into a genuine ecosystem — birds, insects, and undergrowth that a freshly cleared and replanted site would have taken far longer to build on its own.

A newly planted garden looks complete on the day it's installed. A garden built around an existing mature tree looks unfinished at first and only reveals its value a few years later, once the new plantings fill in and the tree's presence shapes how people actually use the space. At The Palm, that's exactly what happened. The tree became the anchor from which the rest of the landscape was designed.

Not every existing tree is worth keeping — some are diseased or genuinely in the way. But when a mature, healthy, native tree can be saved, the case for keeping it is almost always stronger than it first appears. What stands out at The Palm is simply that this choice was made at all, at a stage when clearing the site would have been far easier. It's a quiet example of what sustainable development can look like in practice — not a grand gesture, but a willingness to let one tree shape the plan around it, rather than the other way around.
